claims.text: Thermomechanical processing can enhance short-range atomic ordering in lightweight high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced short-range atomic ordering leads to stable nanoscale architectures.
The resulting nanoscale architectures promote dense, adherent protective oxide or passivation layers.
This mechanism co-optimizes mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to conventional processing.
The studied plates are lightweight high-entropy alloys.
As-cast or solution-treated baseline microstructures lack pronounced short-range ordering.
Exposure at 600–1000 °C and in 3.5% NaCl simulates relevant aerospace and rail-transport operating conditions.
Enhanced short-range ordering restricts detrimental diffusion paths.
Enhanced short-range ordering accelerates formation of a cohesive protective oxide layer.
A continuous protective oxide layer improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The proposed short-range-ordered structural configuration increases mechanical strength.
A stable protective oxide layer improves corrosion protection.
Thermomechanically treated samples will have higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths at room and elevated temperatures than the baseline.
Thermomechanically treated samples will have lower corrosion current density than the baseline.
Thermomechanically treated samples will form denser and more continuous oxide layers than the baseline.
Thermomechanically treated samples will show reduced oxidation mass gain or oxide-scale spallation during long-term high-temperature exposure.
The proposed benefits should cease when enhanced short-range ordering is accompanied by porous, non-adherent, or discontinuous oxide layers.
The proposed benefits may not persist beyond the tested thermal and mechanical limits.
The quantitative property improvements and the processing parameters needed to induce beneficial short-range ordering are undetermined.
A lack of statistically significant improvement, or enhanced short-range ordering without corresponding property improvements, would falsify the hypothesis.
